NVIDIA identifies NVIDIA H100 as its ninth-generation data-center GPU [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100 is based on the NVIDIA Hopper architecture [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA describes NVIDIA H100 as designed for large-scale AI and high-performance computing [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA announced NVIDIA H100 on March 22, 2022 [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100 uses the NVIDIA Hopper architecture [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100 incorporates fourth-generation Tensor Cores [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100 uses the H100 Transformer Engine [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA describes NVIDIA H100 as introducing DPX instructions for accelerating dynamic-programming algorithms [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies fourth-generation NVIDIA NVLink for NVIDIA H100 [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA describes NVIDIA H100 as using second-generation Multi-Instance GPU technology [2](#source-2).

## Specifications and configurations

NVIDIA states that the NVIDIA Hopper architecture is named after Grace Hopper [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA announced that H100 would come in SXM and PCIe form factors [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA projected H100 availability starting in the third quarter of 2022 [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA reports that the GH100 chip powering NVIDIA H100 contains 80 billion transistors [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA reports a die area of 814 square millimeters for the GH100 chip powering NVIDIA H100 [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that the GH100 chip powering NVIDIA H100 uses a TSMC 4N process customized for NVIDIA [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 132 streaming multiprocessors for NVIDIA H100 in its SXM5 configuration [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 16,896 FP32 CUDA cores for NVIDIA H100 in its SXM5 configuration [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 528 fourth-generation Tensor Cores for NVIDIA H100 in its SXM5 configuration [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 80 gigabytes of HBM3 memory for NVIDIA H100 in its SXM5 configuration [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 114 streaming multiprocessors for NVIDIA H100 in its PCIe Gen 5 board configuration [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 14,592 FP32 CUDA cores for NVIDIA H100 in its PCIe Gen 5 board configuration [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 456 fourth-generation Tensor Cores for NVIDIA H100 in its PCIe Gen 5 board configuration [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 80 gigabytes of HBM2e memory for NVIDIA H100 in its PCIe Gen 5 board configuration [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies a 50-megabyte L2 cache for NVIDIA H100 in its SXM5 configuration [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies a 50-megabyte L2 cache for NVIDIA H100 in its PCIe Gen 5 board configuration [2](#source-2).

## Capabilities and deployment

NVIDIA describes FP8 as a new data type for NVIDIA H100's fourth-generation Tensor Cores [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that the H100 Transformer Engine dynamically chooses between FP8 and 16-bit calculations [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that the H100 Transformer Engine combines software with custom NVIDIA Hopper Tensor Core technology [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that the H100 Transformer Engine automatically handles re-casting between FP8 and 16-bit in each layer [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that the H100 Transformer Engine automatically handles scaling between FP8 and 16-bit in each layer [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA labels its NVIDIA H100 launch performance numbers preliminary, based on current expectations and subject to change in shipping products [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA's Figure 2 launch comparison specifies an NDR InfiniBand network for the NVIDIA H100 cluster, with NVLink Switch System where indicated [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA's Figure 2 launch comparison of NVIDIA H100 uses an A100 baseline cluster with an HDR InfiniBand network [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA's launch comparison of NVIDIA H100 uses workload-dependent GPU counts [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA's launch MT-NLG comparison uses different batch sizes for NVIDIA H100 and A100 [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's DPX instructions accelerate Smith-Waterman genomics processing [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's DPX instructions accelerate Floyd-Warshall optimal-route finding for robot fleets in dynamic warehouses [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100 adds thread block clusters as a new level in the CUDA thread group hierarchy [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100 guarantees concurrent scheduling of thread blocks within a cluster [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's thread block clusters enable synchronization among thread blocks running concurrently across multiple streaming multiprocessors [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's thread block clusters enable collaborative data fetching by thread blocks running concurrently across multiple streaming multiprocessors [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's thread block clusters enable data exchange among thread blocks running concurrently across multiple streaming multiprocessors [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's distributed shared memory permits direct communication between streaming multiprocessors for loads, stores and atomics across their shared-memory blocks [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's Tensor Memory Accelerator transfers large data blocks between global memory and shared memory [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's Tensor Memory Accelerator supports asynchronous copies between thread blocks within a cluster [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's asynchronous transaction barriers synchronize general-purpose CUDA threads and on-chip accelerators within a cluster, including across separate streaming multiprocessors [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's asynchronous transaction barrier supports atomic data movement [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies fourth-generation NVIDIA NVLink for NVIDIA H100 [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 900 gigabytes per second of total multi-GPU input/output bandwidth for NVIDIA H100's fourth-generation NVLink [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100 supports PCIe Gen 5 [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA specifies 128 gigabytes per second of total bidirectional bandwidth for NVIDIA H100's PCIe Gen 5 interface [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA's launch article states that NVLink Switch System technology was not yet available with NVIDIA H100 systems [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA describes DGX H100 as using NVIDIA H100 GPUs [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA states that DGX H100 uses fourth-generation NVLink to connect its GPUs [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA states that DGX H100 uses NVSwitch to connect its H100 GPUs over NVLink [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA states that the Grace Hopper Superchip uses the NVIDIA Hopper architecture for its GPU [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA states that the Grace Hopper Superchip uses a NVIDIA Grace CPU [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA states that the Grace Hopper Superchip uses NVLink-C2C to interconnect its CPU and GPU [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA describes the Grace Hopper Superchip as designed for giant-scale HPC and AI applications [3](#source-3).

NVIDIA specifies support for up to seven individual GPU instances on NVIDIA H100 with second-generation Multi-Instance GPU technology [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that each NVIDIA H100 MIG instance has dedicated NVDEC units [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that each NVIDIA H100 MIG instance has dedicated NVJPG units [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that each NVIDIA H100 MIG instance includes its own set of performance monitors [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's native confidential computing extends the trusted execution environment with CPUs to the GPU at full PCIe line rate [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's confidential-computing support protects user data [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's confidential-computing support improves isolation between virtual machines in virtualized and MIG environments [2](#source-2).

NVIDIA states that NVIDIA H100's confidential-computing support improves protection of virtual machines from one another in virtualized and MIG environments [2](#source-2).

## Evaluation and limitations

Aditya Ujeniya coauthored the H100/H200 power-capping paper [4](#source-4).

The power-capping paper describes an investigation of how NVIDIA H100 manages memory power consumption at various power-cap levels [4](#source-4).

The power-capping paper describes an investigation of how NVIDIA H200 manages memory power consumption at various power-cap levels [4](#source-4).

Ujeniya and colleagues describe the NVIDIA H100 configuration in their H100/H200 study as having HBM2e memory [4](#source-4).

In their July 15, 2026 revision, Ujeniya and colleagues report higher efficiency for H200 with HBM3e than NVIDIA H100 with HBM2e for memory-bound applications across varying power caps, in an evaluation using memory-bound TheBandwidthBenchmark [4](#source-4).

The brae project reports using a single PCIe NVIDIA H100 for its CFD benchmark [1](#source-1).

The brae project specifies 80 gigabytes of memory for the PCIe NVIDIA H100 used in its CFD benchmark [1](#source-1).

The report describes brae's benchmark configuration as keeping the mesh, fields, SIMPLE loop, and all linear solves resident on the GPU [1](#source-1).

The report characterizes the benchmark's laminar, physically unsteady performance case as a timing workload with identical work per iteration rather than a field-comparison case [1](#source-1).

The report states that field accuracy in the brae H100 CFD benchmark is validated separately on a converged turbulent case [1](#source-1).

The report cautions that the OpenFOAM-CPU reference in the brae H100 CFD benchmark is not a cost-matched comparison [1](#source-1).

The report cautions that brae's speed margin over the virtualized OpenFOAM-CPU reference is indicative rather than exact because it expects a bare-metal EPYC to be faster [1](#source-1).

philosophy.name: Schematic primary evidence
philosophy.description: Every article claim is a typed factoid with exact original evidence.
philosophy.rules: Use primary sources or original reporting only. Every factual line in an article must render from a schematic factoid, never free-form uncatalogued prose. Each factoid must use the versioned ontology: stable typed entities, a permitted predicate with its required argument roles and entity types, typed literals and explicit units for numbers, modality and attribution, and evidenced conditions, dates and locations where applicable. Bind the entire claim and every structured field to exact quoted passages from captured original evidence. A separate audit must check both meaning and structure; uncertain or unsupported claims cannot enter articles. Preserve contradictions, qualifications and source assertions rather than declaring reports to be independently established truth. Company claims and experimental results require attribution. Classify each source from its actual content as primary evidence or firsthand original reporting; aggregation, commentary, encyclopedia summaries and press-release rewrites do not qualify. Seek material counterevidence without manufacturing balance. Do not infer identities from similar names, geocode place names or invent missing conditions. Human approval of exact content remains mandatory before publication.

review.originalMarkdown:
The NVIDIA H100 is a data-center graphics processing unit based on NVIDIA’s Hopper architecture, designed for large-scale artificial intelligence and high-performance computing workloads [1](#source-1). NVIDIA announced it on March 22, 2022, as the first Hopper-based GPU, succeeding the Ampere generation represented by the A100 [4](#source-4). Its principal features include fourth-generation Tensor Cores, a transformer engine, new dynamic-programming instructions, and expanded interconnect and GPU-partitioning capabilities [1](#source-1).

## Introduction and configurations

The Hopper architecture is named after the American computer scientist Grace Hopper [4](#source-4). At introduction, NVIDIA announced H100 products in SXM and PCIe form factors and projected availability beginning in the third quarter of 2022 [4](#source-4).

The GH100 chip underlying the H100 contains 80 billion transistors, occupies 814 square millimeters, and uses a TSMC 4N manufacturing process customized for NVIDIA [1](#source-1). NVIDIA’s initial specifications distinguish the full GH100 design from the enabled resources in H100 products [1](#source-1).

The specified SXM5 configuration has 132 streaming multiprocessors, 16,896 FP32 CUDA cores, 528 Tensor Cores, and 80 GB of HBM3 memory [1](#source-1). The PCIe configuration has 114 streaming multiprocessors, 14,592 FP32 CUDA cores, 456 Tensor Cores, and 80 GB of HBM2e memory [1](#source-1). Both configurations include a 50 MB L2 cache, while NVIDIA described the SXM5 memory subsystem as providing 3 TB/s of bandwidth [1](#source-1).

## Computation and programming

H100’s fourth-generation Tensor Cores introduce FP8 precision alongside support for higher-precision calculations [1](#source-1). Its transformer engine combines software with Tensor Core hardware to choose dynamically between FP8 and 16-bit calculations, managing scaling and conversion within model layers [1](#source-1). NVIDIA reported potential large-language-model speedups of up to nine times for training and 30 times for inference relative to A100, but labeled its launch performance figures preliminary and subject to change [1](#source-1). The launch comparisons used workload-specific GPU counts and, in some cases, different cluster interconnects and batch sizes for the A100 and H100 systems [1](#source-1).

The architecture also introduces DPX instructions for dynamic-programming algorithms, including Smith–Waterman sequence alignment and Floyd–Warshall route finding [1](#source-1). NVIDIA claimed acceleration of up to seven times over A100 for these algorithms [1](#source-1).

For CUDA programming, Hopper adds thread block clusters, which allow concurrently scheduled blocks on multiple streaming multiprocessors to synchronize and exchange data [1](#source-1). Distributed shared memory supports direct communication between streaming multiprocessors, while the Tensor Memory Accelerator transfers large data blocks between global and shared memory and supports asynchronous copies within a cluster [1](#source-1). Asynchronous transaction barriers coordinate data movement and computation across threads and on-chip accelerators [1](#source-1).

## Interconnects, systems, and isolation

H100 supports fourth-generation NVLink, which NVIDIA specifies at 900 GB/s of total multi-GPU input/output bandwidth, and PCIe Gen 5, specified at 128 GB/s across both directions [1](#source-1). NVIDIA’s announced NVLink Switch System was designed to connect as many as 256 GPUs across 32 nodes; the launch technical article stated that systems using this technology were not yet available [1](#source-1).

NVIDIA announced the DGX H100 system with eight H100 GPUs connected through NVLink and NVSwitch, alongside four- and eight-GPU HGX H100 server-board configurations [4](#source-4). It also announced the Grace Hopper Superchip, pairing a Hopper GPU with a Grace CPU through an NVLink-C2C interconnect for large-scale AI and scientific applications [4](#source-4).

Second-generation Multi-Instance GPU technology supports partitioning an H100 into as many as seven instances, each with dedicated video and JPEG decoding units and performance-monitoring resources [1](#source-1). NVIDIA describes its confidential-computing capabilities as extending trusted execution environments to the GPU and protecting data and virtual machines in virtualized and partitioned deployments [1](#source-1).

## Performance evaluation

MLCommons’ MLPerf Inference records include H100 systems in the Available, Open-division datacenter category, including submissions using four H100 PCIe GPUs and others using five or six H100 80 GB HBM3 GPUs [3](#source-3).

A 2026 arXiv preprint by Aditya Ujeniya and colleagues compared power-capping behavior on H100 with HBM2e and H200 with HBM3e, using compute-bound DGEMM and memory-bound TheBandwidthBenchmark workloads [2](#source-2). In its July 15 revision, the authors reported that H100 remained slightly preferable for strictly compute-bound workloads across the tested power caps, whereas H200 provided superior efficiency for memory-bound applications [2](#source-2).

A separate, project-reported CFD benchmark in the brae repository compared software implementations on one H100 PCIe 80 GB GPU and reported substantial timing differences between device-resident execution and pressure-solver-only GPU offloading [5](#source-5). That report distinguished its laminar timing workload from its separate turbulent accuracy test and cautioned that its virtualized, 24-core CPU reference was not a cost-matched comparison [5](#source-5).
